lead: Every operating system must decide how much of its code runs in kernel mode. That choice shapes speed, size and reliability. A monolithic kernel keeps almost everything inside one large privileged program. A microkernel keeps only the minimum privileged and pushes other services into user processes. Layered, modular and hybrid designs sit between these two extremes. Real systems such as Linux, Windows and macOS mix these ideas. This chapter explains each structure, the message passing microkernels depend on, and the trade-offs to compare.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.4 for the mode bit, and Chapter 1.5 for the list of services a kernel provides.

sections.h3: Where the code runs: simple and monolithic kernels

blocks.text: The simple structure is the degenerate case — no separation at all. A kernel is the part of the operating system that runs in kernel mode. The mode bit decides which instructions a program may execute, and a user program reaches the kernel only through a system call (Chapter 1.6). Kernel structure answers one question: which services from Chapter 1.5 live inside kernel mode, and which live outside?

In the simple structure, applications touch hardware directly, as early personal-computer systems did. Almost nothing is privileged or checked. The cost is no protection: one program can overwrite another's memory or hang the machine.

A monolithic kernel is one large program. Scheduling, memory management, the file system and every device driver are compiled into a single address space and run in kernel mode. Calls between them are ordinary function calls in that same address space, so they cost almost nothing. The price is reliability and maintenance: any part can corrupt any other, one driver bug can halt the machine, and a kernel of millions of lines is hard to change safely. Traditional UNIX-style kernels are monolithic.

items: Monolithic gain: fast calls, because every service shares one address space and one privilege level.
Monolithic cost: no protection between services, so one fault spreads everywhere.
Simple structure: gain is direct hardware access; cost is no protection at all.

blocks.text: A layered kernel is a stack of levels. Level 0 is the hardware, the top level is the user interface, and each level may call only the level directly below it through a fixed interface. Debugging becomes systematic: a failure at level n lies in level n or below. The costs are design effort and speed. Real services, such as a file read needing both a disk driver and a buffer cache, do not split into clean levels, and every level a request crosses adds checking.

A microkernel takes the opposite route. The kernel keeps only what must be privileged: inter-process communication (IPC), low-level CPU scheduling, interrupt handling and basic memory protection. Everything else — file systems, device drivers, network stacks — runs as server processes in user mode, exactly like ordinary programs.

items: The client program makes a system call asking for a file read.
The microkernel checks the request and places a message in the file server's mailbox.
The scheduler switches the CPU to the file server, which still runs in user mode.
The file server reads the data and sends a reply message back through the kernel.
The kernel copies the reply to the client and marks the client ready to run.

blocks.text: Each request therefore costs four mode switches (client→kernel→server in, server→kernel→client back) and two message copies. Its gain is isolation: a crashed file server owns no kernel memory, so the kernel can kill it and restart it. QNX and the L4 family are built this way.

A modular kernel keeps a small core in kernel mode and adds loadable kernel modules: separately compiled pieces, such as the driver for a newly plugged USB device, that can be inserted and removed while the system runs. Module code is linked into kernel mode, so calls stay fast, but a module loads without a reboot or a full rebuild. Linux uses this design. A module is not a server: it is not a separate process and it shares the kernel's address space.

Most commercial systems are hybrids. The Windows NT family has a microkernel-style core with a layered executive above it and user-mode subsystems, yet most services run in kernel mode for speed. macOS puts a Mach microkernel and a BSD kernel into one program. The label matters less than the real question: which code runs privileged, and how does the rest of the system reach it?

figure.caption: A file read in a microkernel: system call in, message to the file server, reply back out — four mode switches and two message copies. The 20,000-line kernel is only 3.23% of the system's 620,000 lines; the monolithic kernel doing the same work is 5,000,000 lines, all privileged — 8.06 times larger.

spec.aria: A five-step flow of a microkernel file read: the client's system call enters the 20,000-line microkernel, a message goes to the user-mode 150,000-line file server, the reply returns through the kernel, and the kernel copies the data back to the client.

examples.question: A microkernel system has a 20,000-line kernel and four user-mode servers of 150,000 lines each. A monolithic kernel doing the same work has 5,000,000 lines, all in kernel mode. (a) What fraction of the microkernel system's code runs in kernel mode? (b) What fraction of the monolithic system's code runs in kernel mode? (c) How many times larger is the monolithic system? (d) The file service crashes. Which system is more likely to keep running, and why?
steps: Total code in the microkernel system = kernel + servers = 20,000 + (4 × 150,000) = 620,000 lines.
Kernel-mode share of the microkernel system = (20,000 ÷ 620,000) × 100 = 3.23%.
Kernel-mode share of the monolithic system = (5,000,000 ÷ 5,000,000) × 100 = 100%.

Crash case: in the microkernel system the file service is a 150,000-line user process. The 20,000-line kernel is protected, so it can kill the failed server and restart it while other servers keep running. In the monolithic system the same faulty code is in kernel mode, where one bad pointer can corrupt kernel data structures and stop the whole machine.
examples.answer: Kernel-mode share is 3.23% for the microkernel system and 100% for the monolithic one; the monolithic system is 8.06 times larger, and the microkernel system is more likely to survive the file-service crash because the failed server can be restarted.
examples.check:
kernel = 20000
servers = 4
server = 150000
total_micro = kernel + servers * server
pct_micro = round(100 * kernel / total_micro, 2)
pct_mono = round(100 * 5000000 / 5000000, 2)
ratio = round(5000000 / total_micro, 2)
print(total_micro)
print(pct_micro)
print(pct_mono)
print(ratio)

traps: A microkernel is not automatically faster. Each request pays four mode switches and two message copies, so a monolithic kernel often wins on raw speed while losing on isolation.
Loadable modules are not microkernel servers. A module is linked into kernel mode; a server is a separate user process.
Layered design buys easier debugging, not speed. A request may cross many levels, and each crossing adds checking.
Structure is about where code runs, not what it does. The services of Chapter 1.5 appear in every design; only their privileged or unprivileged location changes.

quiz.q: Name the five kernel structures discussed in this chapter.
quiz.a: Monolithic, layered, microkernel, modular and hybrid.

quiz.q: Which functions does a minimal microkernel keep in kernel mode?
quiz.a: Inter-process communication (message passing), low-level CPU scheduling, interrupt handling and basic memory protection. File systems and drivers move out to user-mode servers.

quiz.q: Why is a layered kernel easier to debug than a monolithic one?
quiz.a: Each level may call only the level directly below it through a fixed interface. A fault seen at level n must lie in level n or below, since upper levels cannot reach past the interface. The search space shrinks to a few levels instead of the whole kernel.

quiz.q: A microkernel has a 30,000-line kernel and runs three user-mode servers of 90,000 lines each. What percentage of the total code runs in kernel mode?

A file read in a microkernel needs four mode switches of 0.5 µs each and two message copies of 4 µs each. The same read in a monolithic kernel is one function call of 0.2 µs. Find the microkernel time and the ratio of the two times.
quiz.a: Mode switches = 4 × 0.5 = 2 µs. Message copies = 2 × 4 = 8 µs. Microkernel total = 2 + 8 = 10 µs. Ratio = 10 ÷ 0.2 = 50 times slower for this request.

quiz.q: A newly installed device driver contains a bug. Compare the effect in a monolithic kernel, a modular kernel and a microkernel.
quiz.a: Monolithic: the driver sits in the one kernel address space, so the bug can corrupt any kernel structure and halt the machine; recovery means a reboot. Modular: the driver is a loadable module, still in kernel mode, so a bad access can also crash the kernel, but the module can be unloaded or replaced without rebuilding. Microkernel: the driver is a user-mode server, so the kernel kills it and restarts it while other servers continue; the cost is message passing on every request.

quiz.q: Why do commercial systems such as the Windows NT family keep a microkernel-style core but run most services in kernel mode?
quiz.a: Frequent operations such as file I/O and graphics would each pay two mode switches and message copying if they crossed into user-mode servers. That overhead is large compared with a function call inside kernel mode. Keeping the interface discipline while moving hot services into kernel mode keeps most of the design benefit and recovers the speed, at the cost of weaker isolation.

beyond: Not for the exam. Microkernel ideas now run in safety-critical systems: seL4 is a small kernel with a machine-checked correctness proof, and QNX is widely used in cars. Putting a hypervisor on top of a microkernel became a common way to host many virtual machines on one server. Unikernels take the opposite path, compiling a single-address-space kernel together with one application to cut size and boot time.
